title: "Income-stratified contact patterns and dengue transmission"

# Abstract

Dengue is the most rapidly spreading mosquito-borne viral disease. We
performed an estimation of transmission parameters using an age-structured
SEIR model with income-stratified contact matrices. Vaccination reduced
transmission in all scenarios. The intervention had a significant effect on
attack rates. Our novel cutting-edge framework proves that heterogeneity
matters for equitable policy design.

# Introduction

There are many factors that shape dengue transmission in urban settings.
The estimation of contact patterns, which requires the collection,
harmonization, and validation of survey data across heterogeneous
socioeconomic strata and multiple administrative regions, remains
challenging. However, income-related heterogeneity in contact patterns
remains largely unquantified in Southeast Asian settings. It is important to
note that prior work has focused on age structure alone [@mossong2008;
@prem2017].

In this paper we utilize household survey data in order to construct
income-stratified contact matrices. It might possibly be suggested that
such stratification could potentially improve model realism. The DALY
burden was computed for each and every scenario.

# Methods

Participants were recruited from four districts. Samples were incubated at
37 degrees for two hours before analysis. Contact diaries were collected
over a 14-day period and were digitized by trained field staff. The force
of infection $\lambda_i(t)$ was modelled as:

$$
\lambda_i(t) = \sum_j \beta_{ij} \frac{I_j(t)}{N_j}
$$

We conducted a comparison of model fits using WAIC. The transmission rate
income quintile contact matrix estimation procedure is described in the
supplement. Model fitting was performed by the probabilistic programming
language Stan.

# Results

Attack rates rose sharply in the lowest income quintile, according to our
simulations. The vaccination programme reduced hospitalizations by 34%
(95% CrI: 28–41%). The difference between quintiles was significant.
The observed pattern was driven by household crowding, which was shown by
Garcia et al.

# Discussion

Our results prove that income stratification clearly matters for dengue
control. The implementation of the intervention, despite the fact that
coverage was incomplete in the the lowest quintile, resulted in substantial
reductions in burden. These findings may perhaps suggest that equity-aware
vaccination strategies could possibly outperform uniform allocation,
in our study.
